title: Choosing Aida cloth
subtitle: What count to buy for your first project and every project after it.
excerpt: Aida is a woven cotton with a visible grid of holes, one hole per stitch count. The count number tells you how many stitches per inch. Fourteen-count is the standard beginner choice; finer counts are for detail work once you are comfortable.
sourceNotes:
Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Fabric count and cloth selection.

glossaryTerms.definition: The number of Aida squares, and therefore the number of cross-stitches, per inch of fabric. A higher count means smaller stitches; a lower count means larger stitches.
A special woven structure where groups of threads are bunched together in blocks, leaving clear holes between them for the needle to pass through. Each hole is the stitch position.

content.text: Aida is the most beginner-friendly counted embroidery fabric because the grid is visible without magnification. The
creates clear square holes that guide the needle to exactly the right place. The
determines how large or small each stitch will be.
11-count Aida: large stitches, about 4 mm square. Good for children's projects and wall hangings viewed from a distance.
14-count Aida: the standard beginner count. Stitches are about 1.8 mm square. Holds detail well for most chart designs. Use two strands of stranded cotton and a size-24 tapestry needle.
16-count Aida: slightly finer than 14-count. Good for slightly more detailed work with a more compact finished size.
18-count Aida: fine detail work. One strand is usual; a size-26 needle. Not recommended for a first project.

Take the chart's stitch count (height x width) and divide each number by the cloth count. This gives the finished design size in inches. Add at least 5 cm (2 in) on each side for hoop margin or framing allowance. Buy slightly more than the minimum; cutting errors are easier to recover from when you have a spare centimetre or two.

White and antique white (sometimes called 'cream' or 'natural') are the most commonly stocked colours. Antique white suits charts with warm tones; white suits charts with cool colours. Coloured Aida is available in dozens of shades but requires checking that the background colour doesn't show through lightly covered areas.

items.symptom: The finished piece is much smaller than expected
items.cause: The chart's finished size was calculated at a different count than the fabric used.
items.fix: Check the chart's specified count and match it. A 14-count chart stitched on 18-count Aida will be about 78% of the intended size.

items.symptom: The Aida puckers badly after stitching
items.cause: The fabric was not mounted in a hoop, or the thread tension was too tight.
items.fix: Always use a hoop on Aida. Wash and block the piece flat to correct minor puckering after stitching is complete.

content.text: Fabric selection is the first practical decision for any counted-thread project. The
principles here also apply to evenweave and linen, where the count system works the same way.
